macro: Wednesday morning brought a notably cool August PCE print, with core inflation coming in at +0.2% month-over-month versus the Street's +0.3% estimate, and +3.0% year-over-year versus the +3.3% consensus. Q2 GDP was revised sharply higher to +2.2% annualized from a prior reading of +1.5%, reflecting broad-based upward revisions to investment, consumer spending, and government spending. ADP's September jobs report also came in slightly ahead at +90K private payrolls versus the 75K forecast, rebounding from a weak +36K in August.
rates_fed: The cooler PCE print is dovish and bullish for rates, particularly coming on the heels of dovish remarks from Fed's Williams on Tuesday. However, important methodological changes were implemented starting with the August PCE reading that had a downward mechanical impact on price momentum, which may limit the market's enthusiasm for the softer number. Markets are now focused on September price data, with the next CPI print not due until October 14.
market_outlook: Mildly bullish lean on the back of soft PCE and solid ADP, but conviction is limited given the PCE methodology caveat. The key near-term catalyst is Friday's BLS September jobs report, where markets would prefer a soft but not disastrous number — something in the 50–75K range is seen as ideal for yield relief.
bull_case: Core PCE came in well below expectations at +0.2% month-over-month and +3.0% year-over-year, reinforcing a disinflationary narrative and giving the Fed room to ease. Q2 GDP was revised meaningfully higher to +2.2%, suggesting the economy entered the second half on stronger footing than previously thought. ADP's rebound to +90K in September signals the labor market is stabilizing rather than collapsing, supporting a soft-landing narrative. If Friday's BLS report prints in the 50–75K range, it could catalyze meaningful yield relief and a broader equity rally.
bear_case: The soft PCE print is partially explained by methodological calculation changes rather than genuine disinflation, which means markets may discount the number and not give it full dovish credit. Personal income was significantly weaker than expected at +0.2% versus the +0.5% forecast, causing the savings rate to shrink — a potential headwind for future consumer spending. Market-based PCE was actually relatively hot in August at +0.4% headline and +0.3% core, suggesting underlying price pressures have not fully abated. Investors have largely moved on from August data and won't get September inflation clarity until mid-October, leaving a window of uncertainty.
sectors: Construction, manufacturing, education/health services, and leisure/hospitality showed strength in ADP's September report. Financial activities and professional/business services were areas of weakness, shedding jobs in the month.
key_dates: Oct 3 — BLS September Jobs Report (current forecast: +90K total, +80K private)
tts_summary: Here's the read on Wednesday morning's economic data dump. The big headline is the August PCE inflation print, and it came in notably cool. Core PCE was up just 0.2% month-over-month versus the Street's 0.3% estimate, and 3.0% year-over-year versus the 3.3% consensus. The prior July core reading was also revised down from 3.3% to 3.0%. On the surface, that's a dovish, bullish outcome — especially coming right after Fed's Williams struck a more accommodative tone on Tuesday. But here's the important caveat: the Bureau of Economic Analysis implemented methodological changes starting with this August reading that had a mechanical downward effect on price momentum. So some portion of that softness may be a calculation artifact rather than genuine disinflation. Markets are sophisticated enough to know this, and they've largely moved on from August data anyway. September inflation is what really matters, and we won't get that CPI print until October 14th. On growth, Q2 GDP was revised up sharply — from 1.5% to 2.2% annualized — driven by upward revisions to investment, consumer spending, and government spending. That's a solid foundation heading into the back half of the year. ADP's September jobs report added to the constructive tone, with private payrolls coming in at 90,000 — ahead of the 75,000 forecast and a big rebound from August's weak 36,000 print. Strength came from construction, manufacturing, education and health services, and leisure and hospitality. Weakness was concentrated in financial activities and professional and business services. The personal income number was the one soft spot — coming in at just 0.2% versus the 0.5% expected — which caused the savings rate to shrink and raises a flag for future consumer spending. Looking ahead, the all-important BLS September jobs report hits Friday. The current consensus is 90,000 total payrolls and 80,000 private. Markets want a soft but not alarming number — something in the 50 to 75 thousand range is seen as the sweet spot that could bring meaningful yield relief without triggering recession fears. A horrible print would spook, and a hot print would pressure rates higher. The directional lean today is mildly bullish off the PCE beat, but conviction is capped until we get Friday's number and eventually September inflation data in two weeks.
